I. INTRODUCTION The arterial vascularization of the heart is provided by the right and left coronary arteries, their terminal branches present subepicardial and myocardial anastomoses whose functional value is reduced, as shown by their thromboses in the clinic. The veins of the heart run along the surface of the heart and end in the coronary sinus.
II. ARTERIAL VASCULARIZATION The two coronary arteries, first collateral bronchi of the aorta, form a double crown around the heart.

Course and termination The right coronary artery has three segments: The first is oblique downwards, forward and to the right, it reaches the anterior atrioventricular groove (coronary groove), the second is vertical, it runs through the entirety of this groove, and the third segment after having bypassed the right edge of the heart, travels in the lower part of the atrioventricular groove, and at this level becomes the posterior interventricular artery and anastomoses with it. the anterior interventricular artery. N.B: Thus the right coronary artery has a more or less regular coronarographic appearance in a frame or C shape.

c. Collateral branches ? The right fatty artery of Vieussens: is a vascular artery intended for the walls of the aorta and the pulmonary artery. ? The atrial arteries: are intended for the right atrium. There are 3 in number, the most important the atrial artery of the right edge or artery of the sino-atrial node ? The parietal, right and left lower ventricular arteries, intended for the lower faces of the two ventricles. Among these arteries, the most important is the right marginal artery.

At the level of the posterior interventricular groove, the right coronary artery gives, via the posterior interventricular artery, the posterior septal arteries ensuring the vascularization of the postero-inferior 1/3 of the interventricular septum. The right coronary also gives the left retroventricular artery, running in the left part of the atrioventricular groove

Summary ArterialVascularization The heart's arterial vascularization is ensured by the right and left coronary arteries. The left coronary artery arises from the anterolateral left aspect of the ascending aorta at the level of the sinus of Valsalva. It courses anteriorly, curves posteriorly and to the left around the pulmonary trunk, passes beneath the left auricle, and then enters the anterior interventricular sulcus. It terminates by bifurcating into two branches: - The anterior interventricular artery (Left Anterior Descending - LAD): It travels along the anterior interventricular sulcus, then curves around the right border of the heart medially to the apex and ends in the posterior interventricular sulcus. It gives off collateral branches to the ventricles, including parietal and septal branches. - The circumflex artery: It runs within the atrioventricular sulcus and terminates at the inferior aspect of the left ventricle before reaching the crux of the heart. It providescollateral atrial and descendingventricular branches. The right coronary artery originates at the root of the aorta at the sinus of Valsalva. It travels along the anterior atrioventricular sulcus and then proceeds through the lower portion of the posterior atrioventricular sulcus. During its course, it gives off collateral branches, including descending ventricular and ascending atrial branches. It terminates as the posterior interventricular artery, which follows the posterior interventricular sulcus and dissipates before reaching the apex, after providing ventricular collaterals that supply the inferior aspects of both ventricles and the lower third of the interventricular septum. It also gives rise to the left posterior ventricular artery, which travels through the left part of the atrioventricular sulcus and provides branches to the atrioventricular node and the inferior aspect of the left ventricle. VenousVascularization Two systems are responsible for coronary venous return:

- The coronary sinus: Its origin coincides with the termination of the great cardiac vein. It occupies the terminal part of the left atrioventricular sulcus and ends at the inferior aspect of the right atrium. The great cardiac vein or great coronary vein is the primary tributary. - The deep vein system: It consists of two groups of intramyocardial veins that drain directly into the cardiac chambers: the anterior cardiac veins or small cardiac veins (veins of Galen) and the smallest cardiac veins (veins of Thebesius). Lymphatic Drainage The lymphatic drainage is ensured by two networks: a deep network (subendocardial and myocardial) and a superficial network (subpericardial), which drain into two main collectors on the left and right.
